title: Afang Soup
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Afang leaves soaked in hot water two minutes then blended, with four bunches of waterleaf wilted first — and no water added to the soup at all, the meat broth is the liquid.
longDesc: Afang is the other great Efik soup and its two greens behave very differently from edikang ikong's. Okazi, the afang leaf, is tough and fibrous: it gets soaked in hot water for two minutes and then blended to whatever consistency you like. Waterleaf goes in first and wilts in two or three minutes, releasing the moisture the soup needs, which is why no water is added at all — the meat broth is the entire liquid. The blended afang then takes five minutes or until tender enough. Note that the two greens are measured in different units, so the ratio cannot be worked out.
steps: Boil the assorted meats and stockfish until very soft, keeping the broth. Add no water beyond what the meats need.
Soak the afang leaves in hot water 2 minutes, then blend to your preferred consistency.
Add the smoked fish and periwinkles to the seasoned broth and cook 3 to 5 minutes.
Add the sliced waterleaf and cook 2 to 3 minutes, until wilted.
Add the palm oil and cook 3 minutes.
Add the blended afang and cook 5 minutes, or until tender enough.
Add the crayfish powder and the ground scotch bonnet. Taste and adjust the salt.
Take it off the heat and let it stand 1 to 2 minutes on the residual heat.
chefTips: Two minutes in hot water and no more for the afang. It is a soak to soften, not a cook — longer and the leaf loses its character.
Blend to your preferred consistency. Some cooks like it almost smooth, others leave it coarse, and both are legitimate.
Waterleaf before afang. The waterleaf supplies the moisture that lets the soup take no added water at all.
No water in the soup. The meat broth is the liquid, which is why the meats are boiled with only what they need.
Three minutes on the palm oil before the afang goes in. It needs to be incorporated first.
Okazi, ukazi and afang are the same leaf — Gnetum africanum. It is a different plant from utazi and from uziza despite the similar names.
The ratio of the two greens cannot be worked out from this recipe, because waterleaf is given in bunches and okazi in cups. Those units are incommensurable and no source resolves them.
commonMistakes: Boiling the afang leaves rather than soaking them two minutes.
Putting the afang in before the waterleaf.
Treating okazi and utazi as the same leaf.
sources: Adapted from 'Afang Soup Recipe', byline Sisi Jemimah. Native to the Efik. Quantities as printed: 1kg assorted meats; 4 bunches water leaves; 3 cups okazi/afang leaves; 2 cooking spoons palm oil; 1-2 smoked fish pieces; 3 stockfish pieces; 2 cups periwinkles; 1-2 cooking spoons ground scotch bonnet; 1 cooking spoon crayfish powder; 2 Knorr cubes; 1 Maggi crayfish; salt. Yield not specified.

RATIO NOT COMPUTABLE, flagged: waterleaf is given in BUNCHES and okazi in CUPS. The units are incommensurable, so the afang ratio cannot be derived from this page — unlike edikang ikong, where both greens are in cups (NGA063). No source consulted resolves it.
Prep note as printed: afang leaves 'soaked in hot water 2 minutes then blended' to preferred consistency.

No water is added to the finished soup; the meat broth is the liquid base. Cues and times as printed: meats 'very soft'; seasoned broth 3-5 minutes; waterleaves '2-3 min until wilted'; after palm oil 3 minutes; blended afang '5 min "or until tender enough"'; residual heat 1-2 minutes.

ON AFANG, from 'African Vegetables (Leafy Greens)', byline Tayo Oredola, Low Carb Africa: afang or okazi is Gnetum africanum, 'Afang leaves (Ibibio), Okazi/Ukazi (Igbo)', common in the southeast — 'It has a slightly bitter taste when used in dishes. These leaves are mixed with water leaf to prepare Afang soup and Okazi soup.'

A NAMING TRAP, flagged because it causes real errors: utazi, ukazi or okazi, and uziza are three different plants — Gongronema latifolium, Gnetum africanum and Piper guineense respectively. The confusion is common enough to have generated corrective articles.

ON WATERLEAF: 'Efo Gbure (Yoruba)', abundant in the rainy season, and 'As its name implies, it adds a lot of water to whatever dish you are making' — which is exactly why it is paired with the tough, dry afang leaf and why this soup needs no added water.
healthBenefits: Afang leaf is high in protein for a vegetable, and rich in iron.
Periwinkle is very lean and high in iron and magnesium.
Waterleaf contributes vitamin C and minerals.
culturalNote: Afang and edikang ikong are the two soups Calabar is judged by, and they are built on opposite leaf logic: edikang ikong pairs a tender leaf with a watery one, afang pairs a tough fibrous one with the same watery one. In both cases the waterleaf is doing the same job, which is why it turns up in nearly every Efik soup and almost never on its own.
